title: A roll of honor
hook: Var 11 lists the Sikhs of the Gurus by name and town, ordinary people remembered (Bhai Gurdas, Var 11)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Guru bows to the disciple, and your line, the teacher bows. Who did you ask to teach you something? Day seven hundred eight.

On the wall of an old school hallway, or a fire station, or a village hall, there's often a board with names painted on it in gold. Hardly anyone stops to read it. But somebody once decided those names should outlast the people. Bhai Gurdas made a board like that, out of verse. One of his vars stops telling the stories of the Gurus and starts telling the names of the people who sat with them. Today: a roll of honor.
screen: `NAMES PAINTED IN GOLD.` → `HARDLY ANYONE STOPS TO READ THEM.` → `A BOARD MADE OUT OF VERSE.`

segments.voice: It's his eleventh var. Bhai Gurdas begins with the sangat, the gathering of the Guru's Sikhs, and what a Sikh of the Guru is like. Then he does something a reader might not expect. He starts listing names. Sikh after Sikh, Guru by Guru, he names the people who came to Guru Nanak, then to the Gurus after him. Often a name comes with something attached: the town they came from, their family, their trade, a nickname their neighbors would have known. Read it and you meet a crowd of ordinary people. Not kings, not famous holy men. People with work to do and towns to go home to. Why would a poet spend so many stanzas on a list? Here's one way to hear it. A story about a great teacher can make the followers into a blur, a background crowd that nods. Bhai Gurdas refuses the blur. For him, the sangat isn't scenery around the Guru. It's made of particular people, each worth a line, each one named the way their own town would have named them. There's a second thing going on. A list like this is a kind of witness. These people were there. They heard the Guru's word, carried it home, and lived it in their own streets. The roll says: the path was walked by people like this, in places like that. And a third thing. In the Guru's house, a name on the roll doesn't depend on rank. In Bhai Gurdas's list, being remembered comes from being a Sikh of the Guru. That's the whole qualification. Your own town's board works the same way: you don't have to know the names to feel the weight of them.
screen: `THE ELEVENTH VAR: A LIST OF NAMES.` · `A NAME, A TOWN, A TRADE.` · `THE SANGAT IS NOT A BLUR.` · `A ROLL THAT DOESN'T ASK RANK.` · then, large: `ORDINARY NAMES REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write the names of your people. Use the sit to make your own roll. Not famous people. The ones who carried you. A grandmother. A coach. The neighbor who fed you after school. A teacher whose name you nearly forgot. Say each name slowly in your head, and add what Bhai Gurdas would add: where they were from, what they did with their hands. When the bell ends, write the names down somewhere you'll see them. If you pray, you can hold each name for a breath. The bell holds the time.
A roll of honor. Bhai Gurdas's eleventh var, naming the Sikhs of the Gurus one by one, often with their town or trade.
Your line: ordinary names remembered. Today, say one name from your list out loud to someone, and tell them one thing that person did. Day seven hundred eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs read Bhai Gurdas's eleventh var as a record of the early sangat, and it's read and sung alongside the Gurus' bani in some gurdwaras.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: a Sikh, a learner of the Guru. Bhai Gurdas's roll names Sikh after Sikh.

trapdoor: what you thought: a dry list of names.
what it means: a roll of honor. ordinary Sikhs, named with their towns and trades, each worth a line.
what a scholar hears: after its opening on the sangat, the var names Sikhs Guru by Guru, often with town, family or trade, a record historians still mine.

sources.ref: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 11 (the sangat; the names of the Sikhs of the Gurus)

notes: Var 11 described from memory: it opens with the sangat and the qualities of the Gursikh, then (from around pauri 13) names the Sikhs of Guru Nanak and the later Gurus, often with caste, trade, family or town. Confirm the outline of the var and the pauri where the list begins.
No individual names are given on purpose, to avoid misattributing a Sikh to the wrong Guru or town. A Keeper may wish to add two or three names from the var.
howItsDone: confirm that reading/singing Bhai Gurdas's vars in gurdwaras is fairly described as 'in some gurdwaras'.
Editor pass: softened 'nobody stops to read it' to 'hardly anyone' (voice and screen); 'a whole var on a list' changed to 'so many stanzas', since the var opens with the sangat before the names.

Audit (2026-10-01): replaced the vague trapdoor third floor with the var's structure; cut 'a reader can find that moving' for a concrete close. Keeper: confirm historians use Var 11 as a source on the early sangat.
